I told him how earnestly your Grace & every body in England wished to see the interior affairs of the republic better settled than they seemed to be at present, & also that some general scheme for our mutual security might be thought of & be begun upon, butt he said every thing was in so bad a way as to the first, that the last would meet with great difficulties, & would be impracticable without the old recourse of the purse of England. I told him that both ministry & parliament would be most extremely averse to any thing of that kind, as I believed, butt he said without it he despaired.

I had afterwards pretty near the same discourse with the Greffier, with the Pensionary I had none as I am very little acquainted with him, butt the Prince of Orange, when I took leave of him, sent for me into his Closet, & held the following discourse to me, which I think my duty to acquaint you with. he began by lamenting extremely the unhappy situation of the republic, caused as he said by forty years total neglect of every thing that was necessary to carry on government within themselves, as well as their affairs abroad; that he found every thing in so desperate a situation as to both, that he almost despaired of being able to set it right. that the finances were in so bad a way, & the remedy so difficult to putt in practice, the army in so scandalous a condition, tho he hopes he has putt that on a better footing, butt in short every thing in so bad a way that he saw nothing but a most melancholy prospect before him, so much that he assured me that although his birth, his situation, his duty to his Country & every thing called him to the Stadtholdership, yett if he had known beforehand the plague, trouble & vexation that he has since met with, & the great uncertainty he still meets with of putting their affairs in a right way, he thinks he should not have accepted of it, & that if he considered himself only he certainly would have refused it. butt he said he told me this in great confidence, so I only mention it to your Grace. however he said the chief point at present as to foreign affairs was the settlement of the Barrier which with a strong emphasis he said concerned England as well as the republic, that it was therefore absolutely necessary that wee should bear our share of the expense of repairing it. I told His Highness that was a point I had no authority to say any thing upon, butt that in my own private opinion, our country was so drained by the last war it would be very difficult to bring them to consent to fresh expenses, butt then I did ask him leave to putt one question, which was whether he thought, (if all he could wish was granted from England & the barrier towns even in the condition he desired) they would be absolutely secure against the power of France, to which he answered with some quickness, I know your meaning, you think that our places might be as ill defended as they were in the last war . I thanked him for the explanation, & acknowledged that it was partly my meaning, & that I believed more people in England would be of the same opinion till they saw more examples made of those officers that they thought behaved so shamefully. he then talked of the severe sentence against La Rogue; that that ought to satisfy every body; & that the prosecution against Cromstrom
was going on, tho he owned butt slowly from the difficulty he said of getting proofs, & particularly because Chandos would say nothing without positive orders from the Empress Queen, which he had not yet received. then he talked a great deal about the affair of Bergen op Zoom, said it had been greatly misrepresented to the King, that a thousand lies had been told about it, & that, although bad, not near so bad as the world imagined. which latter part of his discourse I own gave me great concern, to see that the Stadtholder who should be desirous to bring such offenders to justice was doing all he could to palliate their offences, & at that time it gave me some suspicions, which, I am almost afraid to say it, & it is to my sorrow that I do say it, I heard in a manner verified in a private conversation I had with a gentleman the very next morning, who said he believed that the enquiry would be dropped, because he had heard that Cromstrom has produced such orders, as cleared himself, & laid the blame too high to admit of any further enquiry. I hope this is not true, if it is, it's shoking to think of. butt to return to my discourse with His Highness, I told him there were toppicks that I should not have presumed to have talked of, had not he began them himself, that I was a private person, had no authority for any thing I said, & only spoke my own private opinion. butt that I could venture to say that you wished extremely that some general plan & practicable scheme could be hit upon for our mutual preservation, by strengthening our alliances. I think those were your Grace's words to me, & so ended our conversation.

& now I am sorry to tell you, tho you have heard it before that the P: of O. is entirely governed by the Princess, & that her Pride, mixed with his obstinacy, have made them generally disliked, so that they have lost their credit with their best friends, & are now reduced to that low servility of courting their enemies. from which you see what little dependence you can have upon a country that has no head nor no government in it. the Pensionary & greffier are both good men, butt the two Benticks, have more power & credit than any body else, butt for want of the Prince's confidence, they have not power enough to do that service to their country, & the liberty of Europe, that their honest hearts desire. the eldest showed me your letter to him, & begged me to assure you that he not only had the highest regard & friendship for you, butt that his greatest dependence was upon you. I do assure you it hurts me to say what I have of the Prince & Princess, as they have both been so civil to me, & I shall ever think my self personally obliged to them, butt your situation, & the confidence you are pleased to place in me, are such; that I should not act an honest part to my Country, & yourself, if I did not write to you so fully as I have. butt I could wish that the greatest part of this letter might be a secret, as it can do no good & may do harm. I shall write to you from Paris, if any messenger goes: this goes by the Captain of the Yacht, Captain William, who is a good man, so it is safe in his hands.
I am, My Dear Lord, your Grace's ever faithful, & most affectionate humble servant,

I received your Graces most kind letter from Calais, and take the Opportunity of a Messenger that is going to Albemarle, to thank you for it. It contained so clear, so sensible an Account of the melancholy State of the Republic of Holland, & was wrote with so much Judgement, and Impartiality, that I could not avoid showing it to the
King & the Duke, in the greatest Confidence. I have not seen the Duke since, but the King said it was a very sensible letter. He doubted, it was all true, & was extremely pleased with the manner, though greatly mortified with the matter contained in the letter, and yet, Bad as things are there, & almost every where else, we must not give up the Game. What the Prince of Orange says about the Barrier is very true, but if we postpone all other Considerations 'till that Barrier is refortified, France will put it out of our power ever to fortify it again. Your Reply to the P. of Orange was admirable, & indeed your whole Conduct in Holland, as right and prudent as possible. As to the Barrier, I see the P. of Oranges little view. He wants the Queen of Hungary to pay them the Subsidy of 1,250,000 florins, to keep a number of Dutch Troops. If that was done, it would only maintain a number of perhaps very bad Troops, but that would not restore the Barrier, & its Fortifications. My Notion with regard to the Demolished Barrier, is this; I look upon Flanders as a sort of Common Country between the Empress-Queen, England & Holland, in which we are all interested; I think the whole Revenue of the Country, should be put upon the best Foot it could, and then all applied to the present Security of it, & to the putting the several Strong Towns again in a proper state of Defence. This would be doing something, & by this Means the Fortifications may by degrees be restored. I am afraid I shall soon receive a letter from you, with a quite different Account of the present State of France. Where, though they have suffered greatly by the War, they have resources, & are making use of them, for establishing a Marine, restoring their Commerce, & gaining all the powers of Europe on their Side, by which means they will hope, & that with reason to be able to impose what Conditions they please upon the rest of the World, without running the Risk of a War, and that is what I would prevent, & I think it might be yet done, & at little expense. We are now invited by the two Empresses to accede to a Defensive Treaty they made in 1746. That I would do, & as the Treaty is purely defensive, & should contain no new engagements for us, France cannot pretend to say any thing against it, after what they acknowledge they have done in renewing their Subsidiary Treaties with Denmark , & Sweden . To this Treaty other powers may accede, no Subsidies will be at present asked, & there will by this means be a Foundation of a Considerable Alliance, which will have its weight, both with France & Prussia. I think Holland cannot avoid acceding. There our friends the Bentinks must assist us. I have a suspicion, that the Greffier, who, by the by, is one of the best, & ablest man amongst them, is not quite well, or in the first Confidence with Bentinck. Groensfeldd is the great Favourite. I hear He is a very able Man & well intentioned. I doubt not but I shall have the same confidential Account of the State of things in France from you, their Views their Intrigues, the State of their Finances, their Manners, their Administration &c. I dare say they are for Peace, but during that Peace they will establish such a power in Europe, as will not be to be controlled hereafter. They have pulled off the Mask a little too soon, by a very haughty letter wrote to Mirepoix, with orders to communicate it to us, of which Alble will give you an account.
I am my Dear Duke ever & unalterably yrs

I know you will be angry with me for troubleing you with what you will call trifles, butt I cant think them so, when the very existence I may say, of two good creatures depend you; I am sure my term is proper for without your speedy relief they actually neither of them can exist. I mean Sr Those Robinson & Hibbins; you know how long I have spoke for them both; & how often you have promised me for both. the first has often laid his scheeme before you, & I am assured it is not only a very practicable one, butt what you might get for him for speaking to the King. & give me leave (as I am used to take liberty with you) to say you ought to do it, consideraing the manner you recalled him in, for you gave butt one reason for it, which was an accusation of a thing that never happened. I, that know your heart, know you to be incapable of dong an ill natured action knowingly; butt indeed if you don't speedily relieve him, you will do one, without excuse. I know you will not like this stile, espetially upon such a subject as this, butt as you know my heart & love for you, you will be extremely in the wrong to take it ill of me.

so much for poor Sr Thomas, now as to the other which is poor Hibbins, I must apply to you in quite a different stile, for him I ask, I beg, I entreat you, to get him a living speedily, for he is actually starving, so much so that by this post I send him something out of my own pocket, for immediate relief. I am not ashamed to own I have a heart that feels for the distressed, & when I cant help them, & my best friend in the world can, & does not, it gives me double concern. forgive me, I am now what I hardly ever am without great reason in very low spirits, for my poor Dear little boy George, is extremely ill of the measles, & a most shocking cough.
I am, My Dear Lord, most sincerely, & most affectionately Yours
I wrote the above last night, butt this morning wee find the dear boy much better, having considerably mended since bleeding. so wee hope he is out of danger.

I have received this afternoon the favour of your letter, which I really take very
kindly, though ire Grace imagined I would not. I must begin with the latter parts of it, which relates to Dear Lord George. The P.S set me at ease. I know the Measles very well. If there is Bleeding & purging enough, there is seldom any Danger, especially in Children of His age, and He was relieved by Bleeding. I hope the Danger is over. However, I shall expect an acct by next post, with a Confirmation of it. As to the two unhappy Men you mention, were it in my power to relieve them, I should be very much to blame if I did it not, as you, my best Friend, so earnestly desire it. However, I will immediately do my best. What is proposed to Sr T. Robinson is an Allowance out of the 4 & half pr cent, which is, in other words, out of the King's Pocket, and I don't know any Body who can make His Majesty give any thing , but His Treasurer, & therefore if Mr. Pelham was disposed to do it, He might bring it about. I can get a Negative, & I will venture one, rather than one moment be suspected of Want of Attention to your Requests. But a Line to Mr. Pelham would really do more, than all I can say, powerful as I am . As to poor Hibbins, His Case is unfortunate, but nothing has fallen, that could be done conveniently for Him. I thought you had fixed upon something, which I suppose has not fallen. If you could let me know the particular Living or Preferment you wish for Him, He shall have my Assistance against all the World, if it has not been previously engaged. I can't agree that Sr. T. Robinson was wrongly removed. The Complaints against Him were so strong, that it was scarce possible to stand it. However, He is a good natured Man. You interest yourself for Him, & I will set seriously to work to serve Him, if possibly I can, & I will do the same for Hibbins. I have been in great pain about Blew . I really thought He had made his escape, or had bribed the Captain of the Packet to carry him off. Three Packets came in, & no Notice of Him, but this Evening, I have received the enclosed Bland Account of Him. I think however, He is safe, & will soon be brought safe to London, so I beg your Orders what to do wh Him. As to our Ministerial Situation, things remain just as they did, & worse they cannot well be. Nobody can tell what I go through except they were to be as happily coupled as I am, and their agreeable Colleague, for His Significance or Insignificance supported by those who should be their best Friends. But I will trouble you no longer upon that disagreeable Subject. I can never think of it with ease to myself, but amongst the many who do not act kindly by me, I must ever acknowledge my Obligation to ire Grace whose Friendship appears upon every occasion wherein I am concerned. Genl Luchesi, Harcourt, Linky & Sussex made a good Meat Breakfast here this Morning, I hope they are safely arrived. My Compliments to the Ds of Richmond.
I am my Dear Lord Ever most affectly Yrs

TEI.text:
Whitehall Thursday morning
Having a bogey of seven inches & a half in me at this time prevents my waiting on your Grace this morning, tho as it will be out by three or four I hope to meet you at the Duke of Grafton's. I send you the sessions paper & am ashamed to say that I did not attend as I should have done to the report, for if I had known as much as I now do by
the sessions paper Paper 47 . I certainly should have spoke for William Fry the Dog horse stealer; for he actually sold him for 10s & 6, the price of a Dog horse to a collar maker, so really as there will be eleven hangued without him, I wish you would speak for him to the King that he may be transported; I know nothing of the Wretch, butt from the sessions paper, nor has he made the least application to me, or any body that I know of; so it is really nothing butt proper compassion that moves me to ask this, & what confirms me in it is that you yourself seem to be of my opinion. so for God's sake don't let this poor Wretch be hangued for want of speaking, for him.
The Duchess of Richmond & I have a boon to ask of your Grace, which is that you would be Godfather to our little Girl. & I wish it had been a boy that his name might have been Thomas. & you'll tell me to day whether next Wednesday evening will suite you.
Lady Lincoln, & a little Kreuningen as proxy for Lady Margaret Bentinck are to be Gossips, neither of them bad kisses, so I hope you wont object to them.
Yours my Dear Lord, most affectionately
Richmond &c. quoque vous me bond quelque foes.

text.p: It is with great pleasure that I hear your Grace intends to be in town on thursday, for I hope that intention will facilitate what I am now going to desire of you, and for which I send this Messenger on purpose to Goodwood. The Duke and Princess Amelia design me the honour of dining att Esher next friday. I insist on your being of the Party, and if the Duchess of Richmond comes this way, I shall be extremely proud if Her Grace would honour me with her company also. It is in your way home, you may take a bed, without ceremony att Esher, go away in the morning as early, or as late as you please, no crowd, no Lady nor Master of the house but yourselves. Our friend Puff and Waldegrave will be there. I shall with prudence and choice avoid any jealousies from abroad, but notwithstanding all I can do or say, that will now and then arise, but your presence and the Duchess of Richmond's will be my protection. Linky is a great Prince & a great fool . He demurs about coming even to my house on this occasion, but I shall putt on the Parent, and command him; I hope you will tell him to behave himself well, for in that respect I have no influence; forgive my Dear Duke, the liberty I take, & let me have the pleasure of knowing that I shall see you, and give me hopes att least of the Ds of Richmond. I write with the knowledge and approbation of my Lord Chamberlain .
I am my Dear Lord your Grace's faithful slave

I suppose his Majesty knows of the death of Lt Coll. Jenkinson, which was a very great loss to the Regiment consequently to me. it happened some time ago & I immediately acquainted His Royal Highness the Duke with it, butt I thought it was impropper to trouble his Majesty with any recommendation before he returned to England, so did not mention it sooner to you. My Major Sr James Chamberlain is as good an officer as any of his rank in the army; & he was a Captain of foot in 1706. butt I will say no more for fear I should break in upon what I was avoiding. all I shall therefore add is that till his Majesty is pleased to appoint a Lieutenant Coll: to the Regiment, I will do my best to see it shant suffer for the want of one. for I really think I need not assure you that I have the good of the Corps most extremely at heart.
I am, My Dear Lord, Your Grace's most faithful humble servant

I have received both your Letters; and will obey your Commands about you Lieutenant. Colonel; and endeavour to do so, about the Living of St. Olav's for little Hughes. There has happened here a most melancholy Accident. Your friend More Freechappel, has killed poor Schwicheldt, the Elder, in a Duel. Everybody is concerned for Him. I am sure, I have Reason to be so; having lost one of the best Friends, I had, in this Country. The King is extremely concerned for Him. More Freechappel is gone off. The Duel was, immediately, occasioned by Something, that passed at Court, the night before. Schwicheldt was as Honest, and as good natured a Man, as ever was born. I am much obliged to you, for all your kindness in your long Letter - But it is only a Continuance of your Goodness. I hope, I am well with the Earl of Lincoln. The Duchess of Newcastle sends Her best Service to you, and the Duchess of Richmond; to whom I beg mine.
